points.title: The Internet
points.must: Definition: a global public network of interconnected networks that uses TCP/IP; anyone with an ISP connection can use it; no one owns all of it.
points.model: Internet = a global, public network of interconnected networks (a WAN of WANs) that communicate using the TCP/IP protocols. Anyone with a connection from an ISP can use it; no single organisation owns it. IP gives devices addresses and routes packets; TCP splits data into numbered packets, checks they arrive and reorders them.

points.title: Internet vs World Wide Web
points.must: The Internet is the network; the WWW is one service on it (web pages viewed in a browser with HTTP/HTTPS, URLs); other services: e-mail, FTP, games, video calls.
points.model: Internet = the network (cables, routers, TCP/IP). WWW = a service that runs on the Internet: linked web pages on web servers, viewed in a browser using HTTP/HTTPS and URLs. Other Internet services: e-mail, file transfer (FTP), online games, video calls, cloud storage.

points.title: Intranet
points.must: Definition: private network of one organisation using Internet technologies, accessed only by authorised members with a login, protected by a firewall; examples of content.
points.model: Intranet = a private network belonging to one organisation that uses Internet technologies (browsers, web pages, TCP/IP, e-mail) but can only be accessed by authorised members, after logging in. Protected by a firewall; from outside only via VPN. School: timetables, homework, marks entry in the e-journal, staff notices, forms. Company: staff directory, HR policies, holiday forms.

points.title: Why organisations use an intranet
points.must: At least three reasons: internal/confidential information kept private, information controlled and up to date in one place, little training (uses a browser), cheap; access levels inside.
points.model: Keeps internal and confidential information private (behind firewall, logins). Information is controlled, official and up to date — changed once, everyone sees it immediately. Staff already know how to use a browser, so little training. Cheap — same web software. Access levels decide who sees what (students see timetables, only teachers enter marks).

points.title: Extranet
points.must: Definition: part of an intranet made available to selected outsiders through a secure login; examples (parents' e-journal, suppliers seeing stock).
points.model: Extranet = the part of an organisation's intranet made available to selected outsiders (parents, suppliers, customers, partners) through a secure login, usually over the Internet. Examples: parents checking their child's marks in the e-journal; suppliers seeing a supermarket's stock levels. Each outsider sees only what concerns them.

points.title: Internet vs intranet comparison
points.must: Matched differences: access (public vs private), scope (global vs one organisation), content and reliability (anyone vs controlled), security (lower vs higher), speed; same technologies.
points.model: Internet is public, whereas an intranet is private (login). Internet is global, whereas an intranet serves one organisation. Anyone publishes on the Internet so information may be unreliable, whereas intranet content is controlled, official and up to date. Internet security is lower, whereas an intranet is behind a firewall with access levels. Intranet usually faster (local network). Both use the same technologies (TCP/IP, browsers).

points.title: Website, intranet or extranet — choosing
points.must: The school example: public info (admission rules) → website; internal (timetable) → intranet; marks → intranet for students + extranet for parents; staff minutes → intranet with access level.
points.model: Ask who needs it and whether it is confidential. Admission rules → public website (outsiders). Timetable, menu → intranet. Term marks → intranet for students, extranet for parents (only their child). Teachers' meeting minutes → intranet, staff-only access level.

points.title: Server and client
points.must: Definitions: server provides a service (files, printing, web, e-mail, logins, database) to other computers; client requests and uses services. Model = roles, not cables.
points.model: Server = a computer or program that provides a service (files, printing, web pages, e-mail, logins, database) to other computers on the network; powerful, always on, managed centrally. Client = a device that requests and uses services from a server, e.g. a student's laptop opening a file on the file server. The network model describes roles, not the topology.

points.title: Request and response
points.must: Steps: client sends request → server checks permission and processes → server sends response (data or error); one server serves many clients.
points.model: 1) Client sends a request (e.g. open Homework.docx). 2) Server checks the user is allowed and finds/processes the data. 3) Server sends a response — the file, 'login accepted' or 'access denied'. One server serves many clients at the same time, so servers have fast CPUs, lots of RAM, RAID disks and are kept in a server room.

points.title: Types of server
points.must: At least five types with their service: file, print, web, mail, authentication, database.
points.model: File server — stores users' files and shared folders (log on anywhere). Print server — manages the print queue. Web server — sends web pages via HTTP/HTTPS. Mail server — sends, receives, stores e-mail, filters spam. Authentication server — holds accounts, checks logins and access rights. Database server — stores a database and answers queries (e-journal).

points.title: Client-server advantages and disadvantages
points.must: Advantages with reasons: central security/access rights, central automatic backup, central updates, log on anywhere, good for many users. Disadvantages: expensive, needs specialist, server = single point of failure, bottleneck.
points.model: Advantages: better security — accounts, access rights, antivirus managed centrally; central automatic backup — data on the server; software and updates installed to all clients at once; users log on at any computer; handles many users. Disadvantages: expensive (servers, licences, server room); needs a network manager; server is a single point of failure — if it fails nobody can use the service; server can become a bottleneck. Reduced with a backup server, UPS, RAID.

points.title: Peer-to-peer network
points.must: Definition: all computers equal, no central server, each is both client and server; each user decides what to share; built into the OS.
points.model: Peer-to-peer (P2P) = a network model in which all computers have equal status (peers), there is no central server and each computer acts as both client and server, sharing its own files and resources and using others'. Each user chooses what to share and sets its permissions. Sharing is built into Windows/macOS/Linux.

points.title: P2P advantages, disadvantages and uses
points.must: Advantages: cheap, easy, no specialist, no single point of failure. Disadvantages: weak security, no central backup, files spread/versions, files unavailable when peer off, peers slow. Uses: home, small office, torrents, blockchain, direct video calls.
points.model: Advantages: cheap (no server), easy to set up, no specialist, no single point of failure. Disadvantages: security depends on each user; no central backup; files spread over computers in several versions; a switched-off peer's files are unavailable; a peer slows down when others use it. Uses: homes, small offices, BitTorrent file sharing (pieces from many peers), blockchain (copy on thousands of peers), some video calls, AirDrop.

points.title: Choosing a model
points.must: Criteria: number of users, sensitivity of data, need for backup, users moving between computers, budget/specialist; worked examples: school → client-server, small bakery → P2P with reasons.
points.model: Many users, sensitive data, reliable backup, users moving between computers → client-server. A few computers, small budget, no IT specialist → P2P. School with 350 PCs: client-server — log on anywhere, central access rights protect marks, automatic backup. Bakery with 3 PCs: P2P — a server would be an unnecessary cost, easy to set up, but owner must back up the accounts PC.
